Equation (1) yields equalities (1,2) by standard variational derivation taking into account the homogeneous Neumann condition for q. We set \(l := \bar{f} / c_{0}\) and \(f := \bar{f} / c_{0}\). If we assume the classic Fourier law

\[ q = -c_{0}\kappa \nabla \vartheta, \] (10)

equation (1,6) yields (1,1). The homogeneous Neumann condition for \(\vartheta\) follows from the no-flux condition \(q\cdot n = 0\) on the boundary of \(\Omega\).

A sliding-mode analysis has been carried out recently for the system described by the equations (1,1)-(1,2) [2]. In the quoted paper three cases are taken into consideration (labeled as Problem A-C). In Problem A, the sliding manifold is given by a linear constraint between \(\vartheta\) and \(\varphi\); in Problems B and C the phase \(\varphi\) is forced to reach a prescribed phase distribution \(\varphi^*\). While in Problems A and B the control law is non-local in the spatial variable, in Problem C the control term is fully local.

In the present paper we carry out a similar sliding-mode analysis, for modified equations where the Fourier law (1,10) is generalized in the light of the works by Green and Naghdi [17-19] and (more recently) by Podio-Guidugli [26], referring to Thermodynamics. These papers introduced the notion of thermal displacement, which is a primitive of the temperature, i.e.

\[ w(x,t) = w_{0}(x) + \int_{0}^{t} \vartheta(x,s)ds, \] (11)

## 3 Existence proofs

The proofs of the existence results in Theorems 2.1 and 2.7 go along the following line. First of all, we will introduce the Yosida approximations of Sign and \(\beta\). In the following subsection, we will make use of the Faedo-Galerkin method, in order to approximate the solutions. Then we will make certain a priori estimates that give uniform bounds on the approximate solutions. Finally we will take the limit of the approximate solutions and we will prove that the limit is actually a solution to the problem.

In fact, I suspect something may be happening in $\mathbb{R}$ that makes the Cauchy problem described below look so simple that it Scott encapsulates, to some extent, how things are in }\mathbb{R}$.- For all $h > 0$, it is possible to find a solution $\uphi(h,\cdot,\cdot,\cdot)$ to the truncated Cauchy problem for equations of the form(eq:x=(y(0)+b*[y(0),y'(0))*Dx)^(*h,y(0),Dx) for all $h > 0$, it is possible to find a solution $\uphi(h,X(0,T),T)$, also satisfying Equation (19.23), that converges to the solution $\ybar \in L^{(2, 0)} (\TT)$. In this way, we can show that the truncated Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations on the torus decay exponentially to either the prescribed limit or the steady state K\({}_{\infty}=0$- The example above is just a toy problem that shows that, in this toy case, the logistic birth/death equation $$Eq:x=\frac_{x-\alpha x}(x-\beta)$$ is an example of what you can set up when you are trying to model sufficiently complex dynamics. Since a lot of the complicated dynamics will cancel out in the solution you might expect to have some fraction of the solutions cycle to get close to the limit or steady state.

### Page 14

.The main result of the proof is the existence and uniqueness of a local weak solution to the underlying wave problem, as well as the existence and uniqueness of a global weak solution to the corresponding full order model. First, we establish the quasi-compactness of the optimal control problem, which is then transformed into a fixed-point problem using the proximal Burgers' equation. Then, we exploit the continuity of the solution to the order when applying the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker theorem. To derive this result, we use backward induction, fix \(\kappa\) and consider the increment made by the operator \(V\mapsto V^{\prime\prime}(t)\), which is from \(\left[m(CH_{\kappa}^{+}\), cf. \(H_{1</frac{12a-32squs}}{a-8}\right]\), to \(\left[H_{1</frac{12a-34squs}}{a}\right]\). Then, we obtain a fixed point problem, where the first component is the integral of the largest eigenvalue, and the second component is twice the maximum singular value. These fixed points based on the half queue role will allow us to prove the existence and unique of the local solution via a standard reduction-to-equality approach, and then proceed to the global solution. This approach does, however, have the disadvantage of not being sufficient to derive existence of a global weak solution, as the fixed point technique moves solution functions via a jump of generators, which results in a nonlocal equation, cf. Shchennikov et al. [36]. Hence, one usually has to make use of regularization techniques for the fixed point problem. To this end,

4 Further regularity

This section contains the proofs of Theorems 2.2 and 2.9. For the sake of clarity, both proofs can be divided in two parts. In the former part we use the notations of the Faedo-Galerkin scheme to prove that the limit function \(\varphi_\varepsilon\) is more regular (in particular \(\varphi_\varepsilon \in H^1(0, T; V)\)). In the latter part, the desired estimates (2.27) and (2.39) are shown for the approximate solution \(\varphi_\varepsilon\). Using the usual compactness argument and the lower semi-continuity of the norm, the estimates (2.27) and (2.39) will follow automatically. In the present proofs, \(C\) still denotes a positive constant independent of \(\rho\) and \(\varepsilon\).

**4.2 Further regularity for Problem (B)**

Since the proof of Theorem 2.9 is based on the same idea of the previous proof, the present proof is just sketched and we will focus only on the differences. We consider equation (3.41) and, like before, we want to derive it with respect to the time. The terms \(\Delta \varphi_{n}, \beta_{\varepsilon}(\varphi_{n}), \pi(\varphi_{n}), \partial_{t} w\) are weakly-differentiable by the considerations made in the previous subsection. If the term \(\rho \operatorname{Sign}_{\varepsilon}(\varphi_{n} - \varphi_{n}^{*})\) were weakly-differentiable, we could carry out the proof as before; the weak-derivability of this term is shown in the following lemma.

**Lemma 4.1.** Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(u \in H^{1}(0, T; H)\). Let \(A = \{ t \in [0, T] : \|\varphi(t)\|_{H} \le \varepsilon \}\) and \(B = [0, T] \setminus A\). Then \(\operatorname{Sign}_{\varepsilon}(u) \in H^{1}(0, T; H)\) and

\[
\frac{d}{dt} \operatorname{Sign}_{\varepsilon}(u) = \begin{cases} \frac{-u_{t}}{\sum \ell} & \text{a.e. in } A, \\ \frac{-u_{t}}{\sum \ell} - \frac{(u, u_{t})}{\|u\|_{H}^{3}} & \text{a.e. in } B. \end{cases}
\]

(4.8)

Moreover, we have that

\[
\left( \frac{d}{dt} \operatorname{Sign}_{\varepsilon}(u), u_{t} \right) \ge 0 \quad \text{a.e. in } [0, T].
\]

(4.9)

**Proof.** Let \(l(t) = 1/\max \{\varepsilon, \|u(t)\|_{H} \}\). By the Stampacchia theorem, this function belongs to \(H^{1}(0, T)\) and its derivative is

\[
\frac{dl}{dt} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{a.e. in } A, \\ -\frac{(u, u_{t})}{\|u\|_{H}^{3}} & \text{a.e. in } B. \end{cases}
\]

(4.10)

By equation (3.6), we have that \(\operatorname{Sign}_{\varepsilon}(u(t)) = l(t)u(t)\). Hence, \(\operatorname{Sign}_{\varepsilon}(u)\) is differentiable by Leibniz rule and its derivative is

\[
\frac{d}{dt} \operatorname{Sign}_{\varepsilon}(u) = l_{t}u + l_{u_{t}} = \begin{cases} \frac{u_{t}}{\varepsilon} & \text{a.e. in } A, \\ -\frac{(u_{t}, u)}{\|u\|_{H}^{3}} u + \frac{u_{t}}{\|u\|^{3}} & \text{a.e. in } B. \end{cases}
\]

(4.11)

Inequality (4.9) is trivial for a.a. \(t \in A\); on \(B\) we use the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality obtaining

\[
\left( \frac{d}{dt} \operatorname{Sign}_{\varepsilon}(u), u_{t} \right) = - \frac{(u_{t}, u)^{2}}{\|u\|_{H}^{3}} + \frac{\|u_{t}\|_{H}^{2}}{\|u\|^{3}} \ge - \frac{\|u_{t}\|_{H}^{2}\|u\|_{H}^{2}}{\|u\|^{3}} + \frac{\|u_{t}\|_{H}^{2}}{\|u\|^{3}} = 0.
\]

(4.12)
